records.table: Springbank 10 Year Old comes from the Campbeltown distillery that malts its own barley on its floors, peats it lightly and distils it two and a half times. Bourbon and sherry casks give cereal, orange and honeycomb with a salty finish; pour it neat, with water beside it.
records.story: Campbeltown once held more than twenty distilleries, and Springbank stands in the middle of the town. By the house's account it was built in 1828 on the site of an illicit still worked by the Mitchells, a family of maltsters who had come to Kintyre as settlers; secondary accounts give the licence of 1828 to the Reids, in-laws of the Mitchells, who sold the distillery to two Mitchell brothers in 1837. The family firm became J&A Mitchell, and in 1872 one of the brothers left after a quarrel and built Glengyle nearby. In the slump after the First World War most of the town's distilleries closed, and by the 1930s only Springbank and Glen Scotia were left. In 1973 Springbank first made Longrow, a heavily peated malt, and after a silence that began in 1979 and lasted into the late 1980s it added the unpeated Hazelburn in 1997. The family's company brought Glengyle back to life in 2004. By its own account the house does every stage on site, from malting to bottling. For a bartender the 10 Year Old is the town's reference malt: light peat, two and a half distillations and no chill filtration.

records.story: The firm of Stewart, Galbraith and Co founded the distillery in 1832 under the name Scotia, and by 1835 the town held almost thirty distilleries, by the house's account. A later owner, Duncan MacCallum (died 1930), is the subject of the distillery's legend: the story goes that he drowned himself in 1930, and staff have long told of his ghost. In the 1930s the Bloch brothers of Glasgow bought the distillery and added Glen to its name. By then most of Campbeltown's distilleries had closed in the slump after the First World War, and only Springbank and Glen Scotia were left, so the name of the town as a whisky region rested on the two. Glen Scotia had hard years after that: it was mothballed in 1984 and reopened in 1989 under new owners, and in 1994 it was bought by Glen Catrine Bonded Warehouse. Through all of it the distillery kept much of its design of the 1830s, by its own account the mash tun, the still room and a dunnage warehouse. Double Cask opens its range for a guest: Campbeltown salt under a sweet sherry finish, and a second distillery to set beside Springbank.

records.story: One of the Mitchell brothers of Springbank left the family distillery after a quarrel with his brother and founded Glengyle nearby in 1872. It was sold in 1919 and stopped distilling in 1925, one of the many Campbeltown distilleries lost in the slump after the First World War. In 2000 Mitchell's Glengyle, a company headed by Springbank's then chairman, bought the silent buildings, and after four years of rebuilding the first spirit ran in 2004, through stills first made for the Ben Wyvis distillery. The whisky could not carry the distillery's name, because the Glengyle name had passed to another company and stood on a blended malt, so it is sold as Kilkerran, from Ceann Loch Chille Chiarain, the Gaelic name of the settlement where Saint Kieran is said to have kept his cell. Early bottlings came out as work in progress while the spirit aged, and in 2016 a standing 12 Year Old joined the range. The revival gave Campbeltown three working distilleries again. For a bartender the 12 is the town's softer smoke, a lighter peating than Longrow from a still house of its own.

records.story: Longrow takes its name from a Campbeltown distillery built in 1824, which closed in 1896. It stood next door to Springbank. The name came back in 1973, when Springbank's then chairman ran an experiment to prove that an Islay-style malt could be made on the mainland: barley peated hard on the distillery's own kiln and distilled twice, in place of Springbank's two and a half times. The spirit was not made every year at first, and it was in the 1990s that Longrow was distilled regularly and took its place as a single malt of its own. The standing bottling carries no age statement and is labelled Peated. For a bartender Longrow completes the lesson of one distillery: the same barley malted on the same floors and the same stills, yet heavy smoke against Springbank's light peat and Hazelburn's none.

records.story: Hazelburn takes its name from one of the Campbeltown distilleries lost in the 1920s, when the slump after the First World War closed most of the town's stills; the sources differ on its last owners and on the very year it shut. The name lay unused for seventy years. In 1997 Springbank, which had first made the heavily peated Longrow in 1973, began a third spirit at the same address: barley malted on its own floors and dried with hot air alone, with no peat, then distilled three times through the same copper stills. That gave the distillery three malts from one barley and one still house, told apart by the peat in the kiln and the number of times the spirit runs: Longrow twice, Springbank two and a half times and Hazelburn three. By the producer's account the 10 Year Old, from bourbon casks alone, is the flagship of the Hazelburn range, bottled each year at 46% ABV. For a bartender it is the control in the experiment: set beside Springbank 10 and Longrow Peated, it lets a guest taste what peat and a third distillation do to one spirit.

story: Hazelburn's first distillation is 1997 in the producer's timeline and Wikipedia; one secondary source gives 1996.
